newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia export earnings dip in 1995/96 on coffee.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia export earnings dip in 1995/96 on coffee.

text.p: Low coffee prices have caused Ethiopia's total export earnings to fall by more than seven percent to $440.4 million in the year ending June 30, 1996, Trade and Industry Minister Kasahun Ayele said on Tuesday.
Ethiopia earned $279.5 million from exporting a record 102,000 tonnes of coffee in 1995/96 compared to $330.9 million from 78,420 tonnes in 1994/95, Kasahun told Reuters Television.
The drop in coffee prices pulled down total export earnings to $440.4 million from $476 million in 1994/95, he said.
Coffee accounted for more than 60 percent of foreign exchange earnings, but the Horn of African country was trying to diversify its exports, the minister said.

Kasahun said that despite the setback from lower coffee prices, Ethiopia's export drive had shown fast growth since the government of Prime Minister Meles Zenawi launched an economic liberalisation programme in 1992.
The reforms have opened up to market forces an economy ruined by civil war and the centralised Marxist system of dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam, who was ousted in 1991.
Kasahun said under the reforms, industries whose output had previously touched just 20 percent of production capacity now worked at around 90 percent of capacity.
Kasahun said that as a result of the liberal system in which the private sector played a major role, the country's export earnings had risen from $178 million in 1992/93 to $275 million in 1993/94.
Ethiopia's gross domestic product grew 8.0 percent in 1995/96 after rising an average 6.5 percent in the past four years, according to the Finance Ministry.
Inflation has been pushed down to below 1.0 percent from more than 30 percent in the Mengistu days, government statistics show.

Kasahun said export commodites which were being promoted as cash crops included hides and skin, leather and leather products, oilseed and pulses, livestock and meat products, gold, qat and horticulture products.

He said although it was not the government's policy to promote qat, exports of the mild intoxicant mainly to neighbouring Djibouti and Somalia more than doubled to nearly $28.2 million in 1995/96 from $13.2 million in 1992/93.
